section_path: Article
text: Mannose-Conjugated Cholesterol Containing Lipid Nanoparticles for Active Targeted mRNA Delivery to Liver Sinusoidal Endothelial and Kupffer Cells

section_path: Abstract
text: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery of mRNA to specific cell types is a necessary task for the development of safe and effective medicines. LNP delivery to the liver is largely driven by the binding of serum ApoE to the LNP surface, followed by subsequent uptake in LDL receptor (LDL-R)-expressing hepatocytes, thereby reducing their utility in nonhepatocyte liver diseases. Herein, we developed an active targeting strategy to overcome this limitation by incorporating mannose-conjugated cholesterol into LNPs. Since cholesterol comprises about half of all molecules in LNPs, we reasoned that it could serve as a scaffold for active targeting. Mannosylated LNPs enhance uptake into liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) and Kupffer cells over hepatocytes following intravenous administration in mice. This process correlated with the expression of mannose receptors (CD206) in LSECs and Kupffer cells, where significantly greater LNP uptake and functional mRNA delivery occurred in CD206+ cells. Higher activity and selectivity could be endowed by reducing the hydrophobic acyl chain length in poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) lipids to induce faster PEG shedding in systemic circulation and increase LNP surface-accessible mannose, thereby increasing binding interactions with mannose receptors on CD206+ cells and subsequent LNP uptake. The results establish that cholesterol can be employed as a ligand carrier in LNPs for enriching mRNA delivery to specific cells in vivo. We anticipate that this general strategy of cholesterol modification can be extended to other ligands and cell types in the future.

section_path: INTRODUCTION
text: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are an efficient and biocompatible platform for delivering genetic drugs that overcome various extracellular and intracellular barriers.1 They are typically composed of four molecules: ionizable amino lipids, cholesterol, phospholipids, and poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) lipids, that self-assemble with negatively charged nucleic acids to form discrete spheres capable of cellular uptake and endosomal escape.2 Because LNPs can transfect liver hepatocytes after intravenous administration,3-5 this approach has garnered clinical success in siRNA silencing6 and Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA CRISPR/Cas gene knockout7 of transthyretin to treat hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis. Aspects of liver physiology and adsorption of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) to LNP surfaces8 has facilitated the delivery of mRNA and genome editors for therapeutic gene editing in hepatocytes. However, to treat diseases in other cell types, approaches to enrich delivery to specific liver cells, other than hepatocytes, are an important goal.

section_path: INTRODUCTION
text: The liver consists of multiple cell types, including hepatocytes, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs), Kupffer cells, dendritic cells, and stellate cells.9 Due to the propensity of LNPs to bind ApoE and utilize the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDL-R), achieving extrahepatic delivery may be enabled by active targeting strategies.10 Active targeting introduces the biofunctionalization of the LNP surface with ligands that specifically bind to cognate receptors expressed in target cells and induce receptor-mediated endocytosis.11,12 The surface can be modified with various types of ligands, including antibodies, proteins, peptides, small-molecule drugs, and carbohydrates.13,14 If LNPs can more effectively accumulate in target cells, the therapeutic index will be broader with reduced systemic toxicity.15

section_path: INTRODUCTION
text: The surface of LNPs has been functionalized through the conjugation of ligands onto one or more lipid components. Prefunctionalization involves first conjugating the desired ligand to a specific lipid, followed by the incorporation of the lipid–ligand conjugate into the LNP. This strategy offers a simpler and more efficient process than postinsertion, in which lipid-conjugated ligands are introduced subsequent to LNP formulation.16 Moreover, this strategy enables control over the density of ligands on the surface of the LNP, thereby ensuring a higher degree of uniformity in lipid–ligand conjugates across each LNP.17 The most common prefunctionalization methodology consists of modifying the distal end of the PEG chain on the PEG lipid, as this site is most highly exposed and accessible on the LNP surface.18 For example, a mannose-functionalized PEG lipid was incorporated into LNPs, achieving the selective delivery of mRNA and siRNA to LSECs via mannose–CD206 interactions.19 Active targeting modification has also been performed on ionizable lipids. For example, anisamide-tethered ionizable amino lipids are synthesized to target sigma receptors on hepatic stellate cells.20

section_path: INTRODUCTION
text: While previous works have primarily focused on active targeting through the modification of PEG lipids and ionizable lipids, cholesterol presents an underexplored opportunity for functionalization to achieve cell-type-enriched delivery. Cholesterol typically comprises about half of all LNP molecules due to beneficial effects on structural integrity, fluidity, and colloidal stability.21 Cholesterol has also been shown to affect LNP liver biodistribution, where a decrease in cholesterol in the LNP formulation can alter biodistribution and increase delivery to the lungs.22 Additionally, cholesterol is present on the outer surface of LNPs, and exposure to ApoE induces the migration of cholesterol from the core to the surface of the LNP.23,24 These studies describing the localization of cholesterol and ionizable amino lipids near the surface of LNPs following dePEGylation further support the feasibility to functionalize lipids for active targeting. Since ionizable amino lipids play a key role in binding and releasing nucleic acids, and phospholipids mediate key interfaces between nucleic acids and water inside of LNPs, chemical modification of cholesterol is an attractive avenue for active targeting using various unique chemical modifications that would be challenging to introduce via chemical modification of other LNP components.25

section_path: INTRODUCTION
text: Hence, we hypothesized that incorporating a mannose ligand into cholesterol could enable targeted delivery to the LSECs and Kupffer cells, which are known to highly express the mannose receptor (CD206) (Figure 1).26,27 We synthesized a series of mannose-conjugated cholesterol (ManC) molecules via modifying the hydroxy headgroup of cholesterol. Linker chemistry was modulated to determine structure–activity relationships (SAR). Click chemistry,28 amide coupling,29 and zinc-catalyzed glycosylation30 afforded different linkers ranging from 0 to 14 carbons in length. These ManCs were each incorporated into a base 4-component LNP system with increasing mannose density. Following confirmation of the successful integration of ManCs into ManC-LNPs, we then characterized ligand presentation on the surface of ManC-LNPs using mannose-binding Concanavalin A (ConA) lectin. Cell-enriched delivery of ManC-LNPs to different liver cell types was examined through the delivery of Cre recombinase (Cre) mRNA via intravenous (IV) administration into Ai14 tdTomato mice, wherein Cre-edited tdTomato-positive cells were quantified via flow cytometry.31 Results from this study indicate that incorporation of ManC into LNPs detargets hepatocytes while simultaneously enriching for delivery to Kupffer cells. We further demonstrate, through calculating fold enrichment in CD206+ cell populations, that cell-type-enriched delivery is dependent on mannose receptor-mediated endocytosis. To induce faster PEG shedding in circulation and allow maximal exposure of mannose on the LNP surface, we utilized an endogenous targeting strategy by synthesizing shorter acyl chain PEG lipids and forming ManC-LNPs.10,32 In vivo studies using these shorter acyl chain PEG lipids revealed an increase in CD206+ Kupffer cells enrichment at 25% ManC3 and ManC5. In summary, the results show that ManC-LNPs exhibit greater selectivity, especially for Kupffer cells, when compared with conventional LNPs, by introducing cholesterol as a modular lipid for further functionalization and active targeting.

section_path: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION > A Systematic Series of ManCs with Increasing Linker Lengths Was Designed and Synthesized.
text: Among the four lipids that make up LNPs, cholesterol is typically the most abundant and plays an important role in the structural integrity and stability of LNPs.2 We also envisioned that cholesterol could be chemically modified to endow active targeting properties to LNPs without a significant loss of activity or tolerability compared to other lipid components, such as ionizable lipids and phospholipids. Considering that cholesterol should present the functional ligand to the surface of LNPs, we designed a systematic series of amphipathic mannose-conjugated cholesterol (ManC) molecules with variable linkers. Conjugation of mannose to cholesterol, in the form of alpha anomers, followed the reactions shown in Figure 2. First, hydroxy groups on the mannose were protected with acetyl groups. Next, the reactive moiety on anomeric carbon sugars was activated with azide or carboxylic acid. Cholesterol was also further modified with propargyl or amine, which allowed click chemistry or amine coupling to occur. Lastly, the conjugated mannose was deprotected to form the final product (ManC1–ManC5). To identify the impact of linker length and design on ligand–receptor binding, we synthesized five different mannose-conjugated cholesterol derivatives. ManC1 was synthesized using ZnF2 as a catalyst (Scheme S1).30 In the absence of a linker, the final structure of ManC1 was rigid. For ManC2, acetylated mannose was modified with an azidopropyl moiety, followed by a click chemistry reaction with propargyl cholesterol using Cu(I)-catalyzed Azide–Alkyne Cycloaddition (CuAAC) (Scheme S2).28,33-35 For the development of ManC3, the azidopropyl group on the acetylated mannose was reduced to an amine using palladium on carbon and hydrogen gas.36 The amine then reacts with succinic anhydride, resulting in the ring opening and the formation of succinic acid. Cholesterol was also modified with an amine37,38 and reacted with the carboxylic acid of succinic acid to form an amide bond (Scheme S3). ManC4 synthesis routes follow similar steps to ManC3. To build a longer linker, acetylated mannose was modified with azidohexyl, and cholesteryl chloroformate was reacted with 1,4-aminobutane to give aminobutyl carbamate. Amide coupling was performed between succinic acid on the mannose and aminobutyl on the cholesterol (Scheme S4).39 ManC5 bears a PEG-like spacer, which was developed from tetraethylene glycol p-toluene sulfonate. Acting as an efficient leaving group, toluene sulfonate was replaced by an azide group, and the alcohol group was oxidized to a carboxylic acid. Aminepropyl moiety on acetylated mannose went through an amide coupling reaction with the carboxylic group of the tetraethylene compound. This allowed the azide on the end to react with the propargyl moiety on cholesterol, giving a triazole linker via click chemistry (Scheme S5). To assess the hydrophilicity of each compound, ALogP values were calculated using the PaDEL descriptor software (Table S1). A general increase in hydrophilicity with increasing linker length in the ManCs was estimated, with ManC4 exhibiting the highest hydrophilicity, potentially due to the presence of multiple amide bonds.

section_path: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION > mRNA-Loaded ManC-LNPs Were Formulated and Characterized.
text: With a series of ManCs in hand, we investigated the potential to formulate self-assembled mRNA LNPs containing ManC1–ManC5. Since ManC can replace cholesterol in LNPs, we prepared a series of LNPs by replacing part, or all, of the cholesterol molecules in the formulations. The base LNP formulation to examine the effect of adding a mannose-conjugated cholesterol consisted of the ionizable amino lipid 4A3–SC7, DOPE, cholesterol, and DMG–PEG2000 with a molar percentage of 23.8/23.8/47.6/4.8, which has previously been shown to effectively deliver mRNA to the liver.40-42 Lipid mix solutions in ethanol and nucleic acid in citrate buffer were mixed rapidly using the vortex method to formulate mannose-modified LNPs (Figure 3A).42 To test the maximal inclusion of mannose without hindering particle formation, we formed five different series of LNPs by increasing the percentage of ManC lipid from 0% to 100% of the total cholesterol content in 25% increments (Figure 3B). The molar percentages of each lipid component are shown in Table S2. The diameters of ManC-LNPs ranged from 80 to 150 nm, with the size of most LNPs being around 100 nm regardless of linker chemistry or mannose inclusion percentage (Figure S1A). Nearly all of the ManC LNPs were monodispersed, with the exception of ManC4 and ManC5-LNPs, which exhibited a slight increase in polydispersity index (PDI) at 75% and 100% incorporation. We also evaluated the encapsulation efficiency of ManC-LNPs. As the inclusion percentage of ManCs into LNPs increased, the encapsulation efficiency decreased (Figure S1B). The inclusion of a large hydrophilic sugar on cholesterol may affect the ability of ionizable lipids to interact with and promote the encapsulation of large anionic nucleic acids, such as mRNA. Finally, we measured the zeta potential of ManC-LNPs, where values ranged from −2 to −6 mV (Figure S2). This indicates that ManC-LNPs possess a neutral surface charge.

section_path: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION > The Surface Presentation of Mannose Was Characterized Using a ConA Assay.
text: Unlike the postinsertion method, the prefunctionalization method does not directly incorporate the ligand to the surface of LNPs. Therefore, to induce active targeting through receptor binding, it is important to confirm that the surface of LNP is successfully functionalized with the ligand. The presentation of mannose on the surface of ManC-LNPs was studied using an assay based on the mannose-binding lectin ConA (Figure 3C).43 In this assay, due to the presence of four binding pockets in ConA, it binds to multiple mannoses, inducing a cross-link-like interaction between LNPs. This causes the formation of a mesh-like structure, and the aggregation is expected to be observed. To replicate the PEG-shedding process that LNPs undergo in vivo, a lower mole percent of PEG (0.3%) was used to formulate ManC-LNPs.44 While most of the ManC-LNPs displayed good colloidal stability despite the lower percentage of PEG inclusion, ManC4-LNPs showed a decrease in stability, resulting in aggregation at 75% and 100% ManC4 inclusion. After incubation of ManC-LNPs with ConA for 2 h, an increase in size was observed with ManC2 to ManC5 (Figure 3D). No change in size was observed with control LNPs (0% ManC-LNPs) and ManC1-LNPs. When ManC2 to ManC5-LNPs were formulated with the original PEG mole percent (4.7%), no interaction between ConA and mannose was observed (Figure 3E) due to steric hindrance on the surface from PEG lipid. Moreover, no significant aggregation was detected following incubation of ManC-LNPs with bovine serum albumin (BSA), confirming the specificity of mannose and ConA interaction (Figure S3). Overall, the results indicate that mannose moieties are indeed present on the surface of ManC-LNPs and that the mannose can be recognized by lectins. Additionally, data suggest that mannose ligand presentation and recognition are dependent on the presence of the linker to introduce space between cholesterol and mannose, as the absence of a linker in ManC1 resulted in no lectin binding regardless of inclusion percentage. Finally, the data also demonstrate the necessity of PEG shedding in vivo for the induction of mannose and lectin binding.

section_path: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION > ManC-LNPs Were Evaluated for In Vivo Efficacy.
text: Previous studies established that control LNPs (0% ManC-LNPs) primarily accumulate in and deliver mRNA to the liver. We examined whether the incorporation of the mannosecontaining cholesterol derivatives ManC1–ManC5 into LNPs would impact biodistribution and functional mRNA delivery in vivo. We utilized Ai14 tdTomato mice and encapsulated Cre recombinase mRNA into each ManC-LNP derivative. When Cre mRNA is translated into Cre protein, it then mediates loxstop-lox recombination events in cells, causing each edited cell to appear bright red, both visually and through fluorescence imaging. This allows for the identification of where functional mRNA delivery is occurring, both on a whole-organ scale and on a more granular, single-cell level. tdTomato mice were injected intravenously with Cre-loaded ManC-LNPs at a dose of 0.015 mg/kg (Figure 4A). Across all different ManC inclusion percentages (0, 25, 50, 75, and 100%), tdTomato fluorescence was detected in the liver. However, an inverse trend was observed, where increasing ManC inclusion percentage correlated with a proportional decrease in fluorescence intensity in the liver at the whole-organ level (Figure 4B). This was especially notable at 75% and 100% inclusion for ManC2–ManC5, where the fluorescence intensity was significantly decreased. Given these observations, we hypothesized that the cell level biodistribution of ManC-LNPs may be transfecting other minority cell types in the liver such as Kupffer cells and LSECs – which only account for ~5–15% of total liver cells in mice – at rates lower than hepatocytes, which comprise nearly 90% of all cells in the liver (Figure 4C). As mannose is known to bind CD206, we utilized flow cytometry to quantify the number of cells expressing CD206 across each liver cell population (hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, and LSECs) in 6–8 weeks old C57BL6/J mice. Baseline data in C57BL6/J mice reveal that LSECs and Kupffer cells are highly enriched for CD206 expression (70–80%), whereas hepatocytes have significantly lower cell populations that express the receptor (~5%) (Figure 4D). We then delivered Cre mRNA ManC-LNPs to Ai14 mice and used flow cytometry to quantify functional delivery in CD206+ liver cells, hypothesizing that ManC-LNPs may use mannose as a means of detargeting hepatocytes. The detailed gating strategies are shown in Figures S4 and S5. Although ManC-LNPs transfected fewer liver cells overall relative to control LNPs (Figures S6 and S7A), when normalized to the total transfected cell population, we observed a significant increase in percent enrichment of Kupffer cells transfected with ManC-LNPs compared to control LNPs (Figure 4E). In contrast, no enrichment was observed in dendritic cells across ManC-LNPs (Figure S7B). These findings suggest that ManC-LNPs enhance delivery to Kupffer cells compared to control LNPs, likely due to mannose–CD206 receptor-mediated endocytosis. These effects were specific to both ManC inclusion percentage and ManC derivative, with enrichment in Kupffer cells and detargeting from hepatocytes for ManC1-LNPs not observed until the LNPs were saturated with mannose by entirely replacing cholesterol with ManC1. ManC2-LNPs containing a short triazole linker showed significant enrichment in Kupffer cells at 25% inclusion, reaching ~70% enrichment. Other ManC-LNPs also presented greater selective delivery to Kupffer cells, where ManC3 performed best at 75–100% inclusion and ManC5 performed best at 50–100% inclusion. In contrast, ManC4-LNPs showed a unique trend where they showed significant enrichment in Kupffer cells at 25–50% inclusion, but as more ManC4 is included, its enrichment decreased significantly. Instead, cell-specific transfection of ManC4-LNPs was observed in LSECs, with enrichment of ~70% at 75% and 100% inclusion. In summary, congruent with our findings from the ConA study and the hypothesis that the absence of a linker reduces mannose exposure on the surface of LNPs, ManC1 required a higher inclusion percentage than other ManCs for observable hepatocyte detargeting and LSEC/Kupffer cell transfection.

section_path: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION > ManC-LNPs Were Evaluated for In Vivo Efficacy.
text: Active targeting involves LNP uptake through ligand–receptor interaction, which ultimately leads to receptor-mediated endocytosis. Therefore, to further evaluate whether enrichment in these cells is CD206+ dependent, we calculated fold enrichment in CD206+ over the CD206− population for each cell type. While no selective delivery resulted in dendritic cells (Figure S7C), an increase in CD206+ enrichment was observed in LSECs and Kupffer cells as the inclusion percentage of ManC increased (Figure 4F). 100% inclusion of ManC1 resulted in a 5- to 8-fold increase in transfection of LSECs and Kupffer cells. A progressive enhancement of enrichment in CD206+ LSECs and Kupffer cells was also observed in ManC2. This upward trend became evident, especially with ManC4 and ManC5, where an 8-fold to 10-fold increase in delivery to CD206+ Kupffer cells was observed. As the ionizable lipid was kept constant across all formulations, the observed improvement in gene expression and enrichment is likely due to mannose-mediated selective delivery. Overall, this data suggests that the linker chemistry used to conjugate mannose to cholesterol influences the active targeting ability, where an increased linker length may facilitate more effective interactions with CD206. Additionally, the hydrophilicity of the linker may induce an orientation of cholesterol toward the surface layer, thereby improving the accessibility of the mannose ligand to bind to the receptors (Table S1). Furthermore, to confirm that ManCs specifically target CD206, we evaluated potential interactions between ManC-LNPs and mannose-binding lectins (MBL1 and MBL2) through protein corona experiments (Figure S8). With 50% and 100% ManC5-LNPs, we observed minimal MBL binding (<1%) compared to control LNPs, indicating that ManC incorporation in LNPs does not significantly enhance soluble lectin adsorption and may not interfere with the targeting efficacy in vivo.

section_path: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION > Receptor Binding Was Enhanced by Incorporating Faster-Shedding PEG Lipids.
text: After LNPs are administered intravenously, they interact with serum proteins in the bloodstream, causing the PEG lipids on their surface to shed.44 It was further reported that shorter acyl chains of PEG lipids shed faster due to a weaker anchor provided by the shorter hydrophobic tail, and that longer acyl chain PEG lipids shed slower.44-46 We reasoned that a lower PEG density, or faster shedding, would allow mannose to be more effectively presented on the surface of LNPs, thereby increasing interactions with mannose receptors and leading to more efficient intracellular delivery to CD206-expressing cells (Figure 5A).47 To evaluate the effects on active targeting of CD206+ cells using shorter PEG lipids compared to DMG–PEG2000 (C14 anchors), we chemically synthesized PEG–C10 and PEG–C12 (Scheme S6).48 10 and 12 carbon tails were added to 3-allyloxy-1,2-propanediol through Williamson ether synthesis. Then, PEG2000 methyl ether is added to the amine headgroup of dilauryly (12 carbon) and didecylyoxypropyl (10 carbon) using CDI, leading to the formation of the carbamate linker. Based on superior mRNA encapsulation and in vivo efficiency, we selected a 25% ratio of ManC2 to ManC5 to formulate into LNPs containing shorter PEG-lipids. The sizes and encapsulation efficiencies of ManC-LNPs are shown in Figure S9A and B. The prepared LNPs loaded with Cre mRNA were administered intravenously into Ail4 tdTomato mice at a dose of 0.015 mg/kg. 48 h after injection, the organs were resected and imaged using IVIS, and the tissues were digested for flow cytometry (Figure 5B). Transfection in different cell types and enrichment in CD206+ cells were quantified (Figures S10A and S11A). Analyzing transfection in each cell type, we observed an increase in percent enrichment in LSECs with ManC2 and ManC3, whereas no significant changes were observed in ManC4 and ManC5 enrichment in LSECs and Kupffer cells (Figure S10B). We also did not observe enrichment in dendritic cells across ManC-LNPs (Figure S11B and C). The higher percent enrichment seen with ManC2 and ManC3-LNPs in LSECs may result from faster in vivo dePEGylation, which exposes ionizable lipids and cholesterols on the LNP surface.23 Additionally, the shorter linker in ManC2 and ManC3 may limit effective receptor binding, possibly inducing nonspecific uptake in LSECs. However, examining receptor-mediated uptake, fold enrichment in CD206+ cells showed a trend where PEG-C10 and PEG–C12 induced more receptor binding in Kupffer cells (Figure 5C). ManC3-LNPs with PEG–C10 and ManC5-LNPs with PEG–C12 resulted in a 6-fold increase in Kupffer cells, which was a significant enhancement compared to those with DMG–PEG2000. This data highlights the importance of PEG shedding in inducing receptor-mediated endocytosis. Although both Kupffer cells and LSECs express CD206, Kupffer cells constitute the first cellular barrier encountered by circulating LNPs in vivo.49 As such, the mannose ligands displayed on the LNP surface could be initially recognized and bound by CD206 on Kupffer cells, limiting the subsequent availability of ManC-LNPs for interaction with LSECs. Further studies will be necessary to elucidate the precise dynamics of LNP uptake among different hepatic cell types.

section_path: CONCLUSIONS
text: Targeted gene delivery is a rapidly growing field in RNA therapeutics, increasing therapeutic efficacy and reducing off-target toxicity. LNPs have emerged as a powerful delivery system for RNA therapeutics in the liver, but the high accumulation in hepatocytes due to ApoE-dependent cellular uptake remains a significant challenge. Stimulated by the recognition that cholesterol comprises about half of all molecules that make up LNPs, we focused on chemical modification of cholesterol with cell-targeting ligands to enable active targeting of LSECs and Kupffer cells. We synthesized five different ManC conjugates and studied the impact of linker chemistry and resulting ligand–receptor interactions. Incorporation of ManC2–5 resulted in the enriched delivery of mRNA, mostly to Kupffer cells, while ManC4 enhanced delivery to LSECs. ManC4 and 5, carrying longer and more hydrophilic linkers, showed enhanced receptor-mediated endocytosis in targeted cells. Although a larger library of compounds is necessary to more rigorously support correlations, the linker chemistry and molecule architecture can influence targeted delivery and cell tropism. Moreover, results showed that enrichment in these cells depended on the mannose–CD206 interaction.

section_path: CONCLUSIONS
text: Considering how lipid components interact and pack in nanoparticles, PEG lipids that coat LNP’s surface may sterically mask the ligand and hinder receptor interaction. Results from a ConA assay indeed indicated that mannose was unable to bind to ConA with higher PEG content. Based on this, shorter PEG lipids, PEG–C10 and PEG–C12, were incorporated into LNPs to induce faster dePEGylation, and the results showed enriched delivery to Kupffer cells. This study highlighted that PEG shedding is likely necessary to allow mannose–CD206 interaction in vivo.

section_path: CONCLUSIONS
text: While cholesterol modification enables an effective path to cell-enriched delivery, several limitations should be acknowledged. The modification of the cholesterol headgroup with hydrophilic ligands, such as mannose, led to reduced encapsulation efficiency due to the steric hindrance introduced by the ligand, potentially limiting overall delivery efficiency. Future studies will focus on optimizing formulation strategies to balance targeting specificity with efficient delivery. Nonetheless, ligand-conjugated cholesterol introduces a new direction to preparing active-targeted LNPs. With further optimization of ManC-LNPs, these approaches offer not only new strategies for biofunctionalization of LNP for targeted delivery but also therapeutic applications in liver diseases related to LSECs and Kupffer cells. We also envision modification of cholesterol with alternative ligands to target additional cells in various tissues.

section_path: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES > Safety Statement.
text: Handling organic solvents and reagents may pose risks. Experimental procedures were executed under standardized safety guidelines to minimize hazardous events. The Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) for every chemical used was read, and appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) was worn throughout the experiments.

section_path: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES > Materials and Reagents.
text: Chemicals and organic solvents for ManC1–ManC5 synthesis were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, Fisher Scientific, or TCI. section_path: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES > Preparation of Standard and Mannosylated LNPs (ManC-LNPs).
text: LNPs used in the studies and the molar percentages are listed in Table S1. The initial base control LNP formulation consisted of 4A3-SC7, DOPE, cholesterol, 1,2-dimyristoyl-rac-glycerol-methoxy(poly(ethylene glycol)) (DMG–PEG; 15/15/30/3, mol/mol) and mRNA (lipids/mRNA, 40/1, wt/wt).50 The formulations for ManC-LNPs were adjusted according to the desired mannose density by partially or entirely replacing the cholesterol content with ManC. An organic phase with lipids was prepared in ethanol, and the aqueous phase was prepared in 10 mM citrate buffer (pH 4) with Cre mRNA. Using a vortex mixer, the organic phase and the aqueous phase were mixed at a lipids: RNA weight ratio of 40:1 and at a constant speed. LNPs were dialyzed against 1X PBS in a 3.5 kDa MWCO dialysis tube (Pur-A-Lyzer Midi Dialysis Kits, Sigma-Aldrich) for 1 h. LNPs were diluted with 1X PBS to a final volume of 200 μL/mouse for IV injections.

section_path: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES > LNP Characterization.
text: The hydrodynamic diameter, polydispersity index (PDI), zeta potential, and encapsulation efficiency were measured to characterize formulated LNPs. Size and PDI were measured using Dynamic Light Scattering (Malvern MicroV model; He–Ne laser, λ = 632 nm). Zeta potential was measured using a DynaPro ZetaStar (λ = 785 nm; detection angles of 90̊ and 163.5̊), coupled to an Arc HPLC system (Wyatt/Waters) for automated sample processing. mRNA encapsulation efficiency was determined using Quant-iT Ribogreen RNA reagent kit (Invitrogen) and Triton X-100 (Thermo Fisher). LNPs were diluted to a final concentration of 2.5 ng/mL mRNA in 1X TE buffer, and mRNA standards were prepared at concentrations of 0, 0.625, 1.25, 2, 5, 5, and 10 ng/mL. Standards and samples were added to a 96-well black opaque polystyrene microplate, followed by the addition of RiboGreen reagent diluted 1,000-fold in 1X TE buffer. The plate was incubated on the shaker in the absence of light for 5 min. The amount of free mRNA was measured using the Infinite F/M200 Pro microplate reader (Tecan) for fluorescence, with an excitation of 485 nm and an emission of 535 nm. Then, a 2% Triton-X solution in 1X TE buffer was added to the plate, and the total amount of mRNA was measured.

section_path: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES > Concanavalin A (ConA) Binding Assay.
text: 0.1 M HEPES buffer containing 400 mM CaCl2 and 400 mM MnCl2 was prepared. For this assay, LNPs were formulated with a lower PEG content (0.3%) to facilitate lectin binding. LNPs were further diluted with 0.1 M HEPES to a final lipid concentration of 0.5 mM. 10 μL of LNPs was incubated with 90 μL of 2 μM ConA solution in 0.1 M HEPES for 2 h. The increase in size due to ConA-mannose binding was measured using Dynamic Light Scattering. To confirm a specific binding interaction, the assay was repeated with BSA.

section_path: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES > In Vivo Evaluation of ManC-LNPs.
text: All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center and were conducted in accordance with local, state, and federal regulations as applicable. Ai14 LoxP-stop-LoxP tdTomato (tdTom) reporter mice were administered Cre mRNA LNPs intravenously (0.015 mg/kg) at 6–8 weeks old. After 2 days, the mice were euthanized, and the liver was imaged using an AMI-HTX imaging system (Spectral Instrument Imaging).

section_path: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES > Cell Isolation and Staining for Flow Cytometry.
text: To test the tdTom+ cells in different liver cell types, cell isolation and staining were performed after treatment with Cre mRNA formulations (0.015 mg/kg). After liver transfection was confirmed, the liver was perfused with 1X PBS on ice. 10X dissociation media were prepared by adding 250 mg of collagenase I (Millipore Sigma) and 57 mg hyaluronidase (Millipore Sigma) to 22.5 mL of DMEM. The prepared media were stored at −20 °C until future use. The liver digestive medium was prepared by diluting 10X dissociation media to 1X with DMEM. 35% BSA solution was added as 1% of the final volume. A small piece of liver tissue was excised and minced using a sterile blade in 1 mL of digestive medium on a Petri dish. Homogenized minced tissues were transferred to an Eppendorf tube and incubated on the shaker for 1 h at 37 °C. Digested liver cells were filtered through a 40 μM mesh. Then, a cell pellet was obtained via speed centrifugation, and the supernatant was removed to resuspend the cells with 1 mL of 1X red blood cell lysis buffer (BioLegend). After incubation on ice for 5 min, the solution was centrifuged again to obtain a cell pellet. The single cells were resuspended in a cell staining buffer (BioLegend) containing specific antibodies for staining (final volume 100 μL). The cells were incubated with antibodies for 20 min in the dark on ice. The cells were then washed with cell staining buffer and resuspended in 500 μL of cell staining buffer for flow cytometry analysis.

section_path: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES > Cell Isolation and Staining for Flow Cytometry.
text: The antibodies used for specific liver cell types were CoraLite488 anti-ASGR1 (Proteintech), Alexa Fluor 647 antimouse CD31 (BioLegend), Alexa Fluor 594 anti-mouse F4/80 (BioLegend), Pacific Blue anti-mouse CD45 (BioLegend), and PerCP/Cy5.5 antimouse CD11c (BioLegend). PE/Cy-7 antimouse CD206 (BioLegend) was added to analyze transfection in cells that express mannose receptors. Ghost Dye Red 780 (Tonbo Biosciences) was used to discriminate live cells. Although CD31 is a pan-endothelial cell marker, additional gating using eFluor 660 anti-mouse LYVE-1 (eBioscience) demonstrated that both surface markers can define LSECs in the liver (Figure S12). The cells were analyzed using an LSRForessa SORP machine (BD Biosciences).

section_path: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES > Protein Corona Experiment.
text: In vitro protein corona formation and isolation were performed following the previously reported protocol.53 Formulated LNPs (5 μg total mRNA in 200 μL) were incubated with an equal volume of purified mouse plasma (C57BL/6) at 37 °C for 15 min. After incubation, protein-bound LNPs were then isolated from unbound proteins using differential centrifugation in a 0.7 M sucrose cushion at 17,000× g for 60 min. Pelleted LNPs were washed 3 times with PBS, and proteins were purified using a ReadyPrep 2-D cleanup kit. Purified proteins were submitted to the UTSW Proteomics core for mass proteomics analysis.
